name: ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct (2018)
dinh_nghia: The ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct (2018 revision) is the primary professional ethics standard for computing professionals worldwide. Published by the Association for Computing Machinery — the oldest and largest computing professional society (founded 1947, 100,000+ members) — the Code establishes ethical obligations for all ACM members and, by widely accepted professional norm, for computing practitioners globally. The 2018 revision updated the 1992 Code to address contemporary computing issues including algorithmic systems, privacy, and AI. The Code is structured in three tiers: General Ethical Principles (Section 1), Professional Responsibilities (Section 2), and Leadership Principles (Section 3).
phan_loai: The ACM Code does not classify violations taxonomically but establishes obligations violated by different forms of academic AI fraud: (1) AI fraud violates 1.3 (Honesty and Trustworthiness) — submitting AI-generated work as one's own is a misrepresentation; (2) Creating AI tools designed for academic fraud violates 1.2 (Avoid Harm) — such tools harm educational institutions and fellow students; (3) Building AI detection systems with known false positive biases violates 2.5 (Thorough Evaluations) — inadequate testing that harms users; (4) Deploying insufficiently secured AI in educational assessments violates 2.9 (Robustness and Security); (5) Hallucinated citations in AI-generated research violate 1.3 (scientific honesty).
lich_su_khai_niem: The ACM Code was originally adopted in 1972, comprehensively revised in 1992, and last updated in 2018. The 2018 revision was led by a task force chaired by Don Gotterbarn and involved three years of development and public consultation. Key changes from 1992 to 2018: (1) Strengthened algorithmic system responsibilities (explicitly addressing automated decision-making); (2) Added explicit prohibition on using computing skills to circumvent security; (3) Strengthened diversity and inclusion language; (4) Added 2.9 (Design Robustly and Securely) as a new professional responsibility. The 2018 revision predates generative AI but its principles directly address all AI-era integrity challenges.
ten_truong_hop: The ACM Code is cited in academic integrity cases involving computing technologies: (1) Software plagiarism detection systems — developers of MOSS (Stanford) and Turnitin cite ACM code obligations for system accuracy; (2) AI exam proctoring systems — companies like Proctorio and ExamSoft are subject to ACM professional obligations of their computing staff; (3) AI writing tool developers — ACM members working at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google face Code obligations regarding AI systems that facilitate academic fraud; (4) EdTech companies — computing professionals in EdTech are bound by ACM Code obligations regarding the accuracy and fairness of their systems.
dien_bien: The Code's practical application to AI academic integrity: Section 1.3 (Honesty) is most directly applicable — it states 'Computing professionals should be honest about their qualifications, and about any limitations and potential problems with their work.' For AI tool developers, this means being honest about hallucination rates, false positive rates, and known limitations. For computing researchers, it means being honest about AI assistance in their publications. Section 2.5 (Thorough Evaluations) requires developers of AI systems used in high-stakes decisions to conduct comprehensive evaluation including bias testing.
ket_qua_xu_ly: The ACM Code provides the professional ethics foundation for computing practitioners involved in EdTech. While the Code's enforcement is primarily through professional reputation rather than legal sanctions, violation of the Code can result in ACM membership revocation and professional censure. The Code is widely cited in: academic integrity policy documents at computing departments; EdTech company codes of conduct; AI research publication guidelines (including ACM Digital Library submission requirements requiring disclosure of AI assistance in paper preparation since 2023).
con_so_thong_ke: ACM founded 1947; 100,000+ members; Code first adopted 1972; revised 1992, 2018; 3 tiers: 8 general principles, 9 professional responsibilities, 6 leadership principles; used as foundation for 100+ computing department academic integrity policies [uncertain]; ACM Digital Library AI disclosure policy adopted 2023; Code available in 10+ language translations [uncertain].
hai_cho_nguoi_hoc: Section 1.2 (Avoid Harm) applies to EdTech developers: computing professionals who build tools that enable academic fraud cause measurable harm to learners who are displaced by fraudulently credentialed peers in competitive programs and employment. Section 2.5 requires that educational AI systems be comprehensively evaluated — including evaluation of whether they genuinely support learning or merely enable credential acquisition without learning. The Code frames student harm not as abstract but as a professional responsibility of computing practitioners.
hai_cho_nghien_cuu: Section 1.3's honesty requirement directly applies to AI-assisted research: ACM members who publish research must honestly disclose AI assistance, honestly represent AI-generated content, and honestly characterize AI-generated data or analyses. The 2023 ACM Digital Library requirement for AI disclosure in paper preparation directly implements Section 1.3. For ACM members building AI research tools, Section 2.5 requires thorough evaluation of accuracy — directly addressing hallucinated citations from AI literature review tools.
hai_cho_xa_hoi: Section 1.2 frames harm avoidance in terms of societal impact: computing professionals who develop AI academic fraud tools cause harm not only to immediate academic integrity but to the broader social contract that academic credentials represent. The Code's societal harm framing is broader than institutional harm — it includes harm to the social value of education as a meritocratic mechanism and harm to public trust in institutions.
cong_cu_phat_hien: Sections 2.5 and 2.9 apply directly to AI detection tool developers: (1) 2.5 requires comprehensive and thorough evaluations of AI detectors — including bias testing across demographic groups (directly addressing the Liang et al., 2023 ESL false positive finding); (2) 2.9 requires robust and secure design — an AI detector that can be easily fooled by text humanizers is not robustly designed; (3) 1.3 requires honesty about detector limitations — vendors who market tools without disclosing accuracy limitations violate the honesty principle. The ACM Code provides the professional ethics basis for demanding higher standards from AI detection tool vendors.
han_che_cong_cu: The ACM Code's professional responsibility framework holds computing practitioners personally responsible for the systems they build and deploy. For AI detection tools with known ESL bias (Liang et al., 2023): (1) The original developers who failed to test for ESL bias may have violated 2.5 (thorough evaluations); (2) The companies that marketed tools with undisclosed false positive rates may have violated 1.3 (honesty); (3) Institutional IT staff who deployed biased tools without adequate evaluation may have violated 2.5 and 1.2 (avoid harm). The Code creates a professional accountability chain for detection tool bias.
watermarking: Section 2.9 (Design Robustly and Securely) applies to LLM watermarking: computing professionals designing watermarking systems must ensure they are robust against stripping attacks, secure against manipulation, and do not create new privacy risks. Section 1.3 (Honesty) applies to watermarking's purpose: if watermarking is represented as reliable proof of AI generation but is easily defeated, that representation is dishonest. The Code requires watermarking researchers to accurately characterize the limitations of current watermarking approaches.
thiet_ke_bai_tap: The ACM Code does not directly address assessment design, but Section 1.5 (Respect Privacy) applies to AI-based assessment monitoring systems used to detect cheating: comprehensive surveillance of student behavior during exams may violate students' reasonable privacy expectations. Section 2.5 applies to computing professionals who build or evaluate assessment AI systems — they must comprehensively assess whether the system accurately measures what it claims to measure and whether it introduces bias.
chinh_sach_truong_hoc: Computing departments at universities have the strongest professional culture connection to ACM Code obligations. CS/IT faculty who are ACM members have professional obligations regarding: (1) Honesty in their own research and teaching (1.3); (2) Avoiding harm in computing instruction (1.2); (3) Thorough evaluation of computing tools deployed in courses (2.5). The ACM Code provides a professional ethics dimension that complements institutional academic integrity policies — computing faculty and students have dual obligations under both.
van_hoa_to_chuc: The ACM Code is explicitly a professional values document, not just a compliance checklist — it is designed to inculcate professional culture in computing practitioners from their earliest training. Computer science education programs use the Code to socialize students into professional ethics norms. This culture-building function parallels McCabe's honor culture approach to academic integrity: the goal is professional identity formation, not just rule compliance.
ai_literacy: The ACM Code's professional development obligations (Section 2.6: Perform Work Only in Areas of Competence) imply that computing professionals must maintain competency in AI ethics as AI becomes central to their work. For EdTech practitioners specifically, competency in AI ethics includes understanding AI limitations, bias risks, and integrity implications — the components of AI literacy. The Code requires that computing professionals continually update their understanding of the systems they build, which in 2024-2026 means understanding generative AI characteristics including hallucination and bias.
khung_quoc_te: The ACM Code is the primary professional ethics standard for computing — distinct from but complementary to UNESCO 2021 (government), EU AI Act 2024 (law), and IEEE EAD 2019 (engineering standards). ACM Code Section 1.3 (Honesty) implements the same value as UNESCO Honesty/Transparency principles and ICAI Honesty value in a professional context. The Code's Section 1.2 (Avoid Harm) parallels UNESCO's 'Do No Harm' principle and IEEE's 'Human Well-being' principle. ACM and IEEE Codes together cover the professional obligations of computing practitioners; UNESCO and EU Act cover governmental obligations.
phap_luat_viet_nam: ACM membership and Code obligations apply to Vietnamese computing professionals who are ACM members. Vietnam has a growing ACM membership through universities like HCMUS, VNU, HUST, and FPT University. Vietnamese computing faculty and researchers who are ACM members have professional obligations under the Code — including honesty in AI-assisted research. Vietnam's domestic computing professional organizations (VAIP — Vietnam Association for Information Processing) have their own codes of conduct but have not formally aligned with ACM Code [uncertain: exact VAIP code content].
chinh_sach_chau_a: ACM has 30+ chapters across Asia including active chapters in Vietnam (HCMUS ACM Student Chapter, VNU ACM Chapter), Singapore (NUS ACM Chapter), South Korea, Japan, and India. ACM Code obligations apply to all chapter members. ACM's Asia computing education conferences (SIGCSE Asia-Pacific) have addressed AI academic integrity. The NUS School of Computing requires CS students to understand ACM Code obligations as part of the professional ethics curriculum — integrating Code compliance with academic integrity education.
ai_tutor_vs_ai_cheater: The ACM Code's honesty principle provides a professional ethics resolution: AI functions as a legitimate tutor when its use is disclosed (Section 1.3) and the student retains genuine cognitive responsibility; AI functions as a cheating tool when students use it to misrepresent their capabilities. For computing professionals building AI tools, Section 1.2 creates a design obligation: do not build tools whose primary use case is enabling academic fraud. The tutor/cheater distinction maps to the ACM professional obligation to consider 'all reasonably foreseeable uses' of a system.
edtech_company_policies: Computing professionals employed by EdTech companies are bound by ACM Code obligations in their professional work: (1) Khan Academy developers — Section 1.2 obligations to avoid harm in educational AI design; Khanmigo's Socratic design reflects Code-consistent harm avoidance; (2) Turnitin developers — Section 2.5 obligations to evaluate AI detector accuracy including bias testing; (3) OpenAI/Anthropic engineers — Section 1.2 obligations regarding AI systems that enable academic fraud; (4) Duolingo engineers — Section 2.9 obligations for secure, robust AI design in educational assessments. The ACM Code applies to individual practitioners, not just companies.
de_xuat_nha_nghien_cuu: Applying ACM Code to EdTech AI integrity research: (1) Use Sections 1.3 and 2.5 to create an ethical audit framework for AI detection tools deployed in Vietnamese universities — requiring vendors to document accuracy, bias characteristics, and limitations; (2) Propose that Vietnamese computing professional organizations (VAIP) adopt ACM Code-aligned standards for EdTech AI practitioners; (3) Design AI literacy curricula for computing students that explicitly incorporate ACM Code ethics alongside technical AI education; (4) Use Section 1.2 (Avoid Harm) to argue for computing practitioners' professional responsibility in the AI academic fraud ecosystem — developers, deployers, and users all share ethical obligations; (5) Recommend that HCMUS and VNU computing programs include ACM Code analysis of AI integrity cases as a mandatory component of professional ethics courses.

nguon_viet_nam: ACM Student Chapters exist at HCMUS and VNU — chapter members are subject to ACM Code obligations. Vietnamese computing education programs at HCMUS, VNU-HCMUT, and HUST include professional ethics modules that may reference ACM Code [uncertain: which programs explicitly teach ACM Code]. The ACM Code is available in Vietnamese translation [uncertain: whether official Vietnamese translation exists]. VAIP (Vietnam Association for Information Processing) is the domestic professional body but its code of conduct relationship to ACM Code has not been formally documented.
